vignette:
Youssef is a 55-year-old Jordanian-American man who has farmed a small plot of land in the Central Valley of California for nearly two decades. He is married, the father of three adult children, and until roughly eighteen months ago was known among his neighbours and at the local farmers' cooperative as a steady, unhurried presence - a man who rose before dawn and worked until the light failed without complaint. He presented for an intake appointment after his wife, increasingly alarmed by changes she had watched accumulate since the assault, told him plainly that she did not recognise him anymore.

The assault occurred on a Tuesday evening in late autumn, when Youssef had stayed past dark to repair a section of irrigation pipe at the far edge of his property. Two men approached him from behind the equipment shed. What followed was a prolonged beating - fists, then boots - that left him with a fractured orbital socket, broken ribs, and a period of unconsciousness whose length he still cannot account for. He remembers the physical closeness of the men, the heat and smell of their exertion, and the particular rhythm of his own heart hammering in his chest in the seconds before the first blow landed. He does not remember how he got back to the farmhouse. His wife found him on the porch steps.

In the weeks after the assault, Youssef noticed that his memory of the event did not settle into a coherent story the way he expected it to. When he tried to tell his wife what had happened - something she asked for gently, repeatedly, because the police report required his account - he would begin and then lose the thread entirely, sometimes stopping mid-sentence, sometimes trailing into silence. The memory did not feel like something that had happened to him. It felt, he told his intake clinician, like footage from a film he had watched once and half-forgotten, something witnessed rather than lived. The pieces came to him out of sequence and without connective tissue: a boot sole, a shadow moving, the cold of the ground, his own pulse - but no narrative that held them together.

Certain things in his daily life became unbearable in ways he could not always anticipate. Because he works physically demanding hours on the farm, his heart rate climbs naturally during irrigation runs, fence repairs, and the loading of produce onto the truck bed. Each time his pulse quickened, Youssef found himself arrested mid-task, certain in a way that bypassed reasoning that something was about to happen to him. The smell of another man's sweat - common enough among the seasonal labourers who work alongside him - produced the same arrest. He had come to believe, without being able to fully articulate why, that his body was a more reliable warning system than his mind, and so he monitored it constantly. When a stranger lingered too long near the equipment shed, or when a worker he did not know well moved in a way that struck him as purposeless or watchful, he was certain the threat was real and immediate.

Over the following months, Youssef began arriving at the farm earlier and staying later, filling every available hour with physical work. His wife noted that he had stopped eating dinner with the family most evenings. He had also quietly rearranged the calendar of the cooperative's monthly meetings so that he was never present on the Tuesday closest to the anniversary of the assault, offering logistical excuses that his fellow farmers accepted without question. He spent considerable time - lying awake, driving between fields - turning over in his mind what he should have done to the men, what he might still do, rehearsing confrontations in elaborate detail. These thoughts brought him no relief, but he returned to them compulsively, as though the problem they addressed remained unsolved.

What finally brought him to the clinic was not a single event but an accumulation: a season in which the harvest had gone well by every external measure and he had felt nothing. His wife had wept at the dinner table one evening and said she was frightened for him. Youssef sat in the intake session with his hands folded and his expression carefully composed. What he feared most, he said quietly, was that the man who had worked this land for eighteen years was simply gone. What he hoped for, with considerably less certainty, was that this was not true.
